title: k6 tutorial: captured traffic with mocked backends
summary: Capture API traffic with Speedscale, export a k6 load scenario, and mock backend dependencies in Kubernetes with speedctl or locally with proxymock.
body_markdown:
Point k6 at a service with live dependencies and you end up load testing the dependencies: their rate limits, their shared test data, their bad day. This tutorial captures requests with Speedscale, converts the inbound traffic into a k6 scenario, and uses the recorded outbound traffic to mock the backends. k6 drives the real application, the application calls recorded dependencies, and the numbers you get describe your service.


We’ll use the[NGINX demo](https://github.com/speedscale/demo/tree/0ad18e83e93008f45e68b5d67879412bb050e8f2/nginx) . Its gateway forwards` /payment/` to the payment service. You’ll capture that exchange once, then run the same k6 scenario against the gateway in Kubernetes or in Docker on your laptop. Capture and the k6 conversion are shared. After that, pick one path:mock in Kubernetes with speedctl ormock locally with proxymock . You don’t need both.


```text
flowchart TB
C[Speedscale capture] --> S[Snapshot: inbound and outbound traffic]
S --> E[Export inbound requests to k6]
S --> M[Recorded backend responses]
E --> K[k6 load scenario]
K --> A[Real NGINX gateway]
A --> R[Backend mocks]
M --> R
R --- B[speedctl in Kubernetes or proxymock locally]


```


## Before you start


You need Docker, Git, Python 3, jq, kubectl, k6, and an initialized` speedctl` . For the local option, install and initialize` proxymock` for the same Speedscale account. Follow the[k6 installation guide](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/set-up/install-k6/) ,[Speedscale Operator installation guide](https://docs.speedscale.com/setup/install/kubernetes-operator/) , and[proxymock quickstart](https://docs.speedscale.com/proxymock/getting-started/quickstart/quickstart-cli/) if these aren’t installed.


Use a development cluster with an active Speedscale inspector. The cluster path requires Speedscale v2.5.789 or newer and` speedctl` v2.5.833 or newer for the mock readiness check. Use a current` proxymock` with` --no-passthrough` support. Port 8080 must be free on your machine for either path. The local path also needs 18081, plus` proxymock` ’s default listener ports 4140 and 4145. The local Docker commands work on Docker Desktop;` --add-host` also supplies the host gateway mapping on Linux. These examples were tested with Speedscale v2.5.1171,` speedctl` v2.5.1059,` proxymock` v2.5.1133, k6 v2.2.0, and NGINX 1.27.5.


Set these variables in the terminal where you run the tutorial.` CLUSTER` is the cluster name registered in Speedscale;` KUBE_CONTEXT` is its kubectl context. They can differ. Substitute your own values, then confirm they refer to the same development cluster:


```text
export   KUBE_CONTEXT  =  minikube
export   CLUSTER  =  demo-cluster
export   NAMESPACE  =  k6-tutorial
kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   get   nodes
speedctl   infra   inspectors   -o   pretty
```


## Capture traffic with Speedscale


Clone the pinned demo revision into a new directory. Deploy its services without the demo’s background traffic generator:


```text
git   clone   https://github.com/speedscale/demo.git   k6-demo
cd   k6-demo
git   checkout   0ad18e83e93008f45e68b5d67879412bb050e8f2
mkdir   k6-workflow
cd   k6-workflow


kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   create   namespace   "  $NAMESPACE  "
kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   apply   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   \
-f   ../nginx/base/gateway.yaml   \
-f   ../nginx/base/payment.yaml   \
-f   ../nginx/base/user.yaml


kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   annotate   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   deployment/gateway   \
sidecar.speedscale.com/inject=  true   \
sidecar.speedscale.com/capture-mode=proxy   \
sidecar.speedscale.com/proxy-type=transparent


kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   rollout   status   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   deployment/payment   --timeout=120s
kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   rollout   status   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   deployment/user   --timeout=120s
kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   rollout   status   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   deployment/gateway   --timeout=120s
```


NGINX resolves both the payment and user upstreams when it starts, so deploy both even though this test uses only payment. Generate the capture request from inside the cluster. This also avoids recording a loopback port-forward connection as outbound traffic:


```text
kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   run   k6-capture   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   \
--image=curlimages/curl:8.12.1   --restart=Never   --command   --   \
curl   --fail   --silent   --show-error   http://gateway/payment/
kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   wait   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   pod/k6-capture   \
--for=jsonpath=  '{.status.phase}'  =Succeeded   --timeout=90s
kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   logs   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   k6-capture
```


The response is:


```text
{  "status"  :   "ok"  ,   "service"  :   "payment"  ,   "version"  :   "1.0"  }
```


In Speedscale’s Traffic Viewer, filter to this cluster, namespace, and gateway service. Confirm you see the inbound` GET /payment/` and the outbound` GET /` to` payment:80` before creating a snapshot. Both directions must be present: the inbound request becomes the k6 test, and the outbound response becomes the backend mock. If traffic hasn’t arrived yet, wait for collection before continuing.


Save the filtered traffic in the dashboard, or create the same snapshot with the CLI:


```text
SNAPSHOT_ID  =  $(  speedctl   create   snapshot   \
--name   k6-gateway-payment   \
--service   gateway   \
--filter   "(cluster IS   \"  $CLUSTER  \"  ) AND (namespace IS   \"  $NAMESPACE  \"  ) AND (service IS   \"  gateway  \"  )"   \
--start   5m   -o   json   |   jq   -er   '.snapshot.id'  )
export   SNAPSHOT_ID
speedctl   wait   snapshot   "  $SNAPSHOT_ID  "   --timeout   3m
```


Keep the snapshot limited to this route for the tutorial’s payment-specific assertions. For your own application,[mask sensitive data](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/dlp/) and review authentication and dynamic values before exporting traffic.


## Convert the snapshot into a k6 load scenario


[Export the snapshot to k6](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/integrations/export/grafana/) , including only inbound requests. The snapshot itself keeps both directions:


```text
speedctl   export   snapshot   "  $SNAPSHOT_ID  "   \
--type   k6   --inbound-only   --output   recorded.js
```


Open` recorded.js` and confirm it contains a` GET` for` /payment/` . An empty iteration function means the snapshot has no eligible inbound HTTP requests. Stop and correct the capture before proceeding. This export handles HTTP and HTTPS requests; captured database calls belong in the backend mocks.


The exporter preserves recorded requests but doesn’t add a load profile or application assertions. Save the following as` prepare-k6.py` . It keeps` recorded.js` unchanged and writes` k6.js` with a configurable target, five virtual users for 30 seconds, and checks for the payment response:


```text
from   pathlib   import   Path


source   =   Path(  'recorded.js'  ).read_text()
call   =   'http.request(method, url.toString(), body, params);'
if   call   not   in   source:
raise   SystemExit  (  'Exporter format changed: review recorded.js before adapting it.'  )


extra   =   '''
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';


if (!__ENV.BASE_URL) {
throw new Error('Set BASE_URL to the application URL.');
}
const target = new URL(__ENV.BASE_URL);
if (!['http:', 'https:'].includes(target.protocol) || target.pathname !== '/' || target.search || target.hash) {
throw new Error('BASE_URL must be an HTTP(S) origin without a path, query, or fragment.');
}


export const options = {
scenarios: {
recorded_traffic: {
executor: 'constant-vus',
vus: 5,
duration: '30s',
gracefulStop: '5s',
},
},
thresholds: {
http_reqs: ['count>0'],
iterations: ['count>0'],
http_req_failed: ['rate==0'],
checks: ['rate==1'],
http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500'],
},
};


function requestWithChecks(method, recordedURL, body, params) {
const url = new URL(recordedURL);
url.protocol = target.protocol;
url.hostname = target.hostname;
url.port = target.port;
for (const key of Object.keys(params.headers)) {
if (['host', 'connection', 'content-length'].includes(key.toLowerCase())) {
delete params.headers[key];
}
}
params.timeout = '5s';
const response = http.request(method, url.toString(), body, params);
check(response, {
'HTTP 200': (r) => r.status === 200,
'payment response': (r) => {
try {
const data = r.json();
return data.status === 'ok' && data.service === 'payment' && data.version === '1.0';
} catch (_) {
return false;
}
},
});
}
'''


marker   =   'export default function () {'
if   source.count(marker)   !=   1  :
raise   SystemExit  (  'Expected exactly one exported iteration function.'  )
source   =   source.replace(call,   'requestWithChecks(method, url.toString(), body, params);'  )
source   =   source.replace(marker, extra   +   '  \n  '   +   marker,   1  )
last_brace   =   source.rfind(  '}'  )
source   =   source[:last_brace]   +   '  sleep(1);  \n  '   +   source[last_brace:]
Path(  'k6.js'  ).write_text(source)
print  (  'Wrote k6.js; recorded.js is unchanged.'  )
```


Run the conversion:


```text
python3   prepare-k6.py
k6   inspect   --env   BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080   k6.js
```


The conversion changes each request’s scheme, hostname, and port. It preserves the method, path, query parameters, body, and other headers. Removing the recorded` Host` header lets k6 address the new target correctly. If your application depends on virtual-host routing, supply its required Host header explicitly instead.


One iteration runs the complete exported request sequence, then sleeps for one second. Five VUs is concurrent activity, not a fixed requests-per-second rate. A larger snapshot sends more requests per iteration. Start small and set your load model deliberately; this export doesn’t reconstruct session correlations or refresh expired credentials.


The thresholds require completed requests and iterations. They also make a failed request, failed body check, or p95 latency of 500 ms or more return a nonzero k6 exit code. Each request has a five-second timeout. That latency budget is an example for this demo; set it to your application’s SLO.[k6 checks need thresholds](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/thresholds/) to fail the run.


## Mock backends in Kubernetes with speedctl


For k6 to supply all inbound traffic, start a Speedscale replay in` responder-only` mode.` --mock-only` selects dependencies and doesn’t disable Speedscale’s traffic generator. Save this as` external-driver.json` :


```text
{
"id"  :   "k6-tutorial-external-driver"  ,
"protected"  :   false  ,
"generator"  : {
"stages"  : [
{
"virtualUsers"  : {
"virtualUsers"  :   "1"  ,
"requestDelay"  : {}
}
}
]
},
"rules"  : [],
"version"  :   3  ,
"assertionGroups"  : [],
"responder"  : {
"numReplicas"  :   1  ,
"passthrough_mode"  :   false  ,
"with_report"  :   true
},
"cluster"  : {
"replayMode"  :   "responder-only"  ,
"logsCollected"  :   false  ,
"sidecar_tls_out"  :   true  ,
"cleanup"  :   "inventory"  ,
"logLevel"  :   "info"
}
}
```


Upload the config:


```text
speedctl   put   testconfig   external-driver.json
```


` passthrough_mode: false` makes an unmatched backend request fail instead of reaching the live payment service. The operator attaches the recorded outbound mocks to the gateway. Follow the[external driver lifecycle](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/replay/via-speedctl/#wait-for-service-mocks) : start mocks, wait for readiness, start a fresh port-forward, run k6, and cancel the replay.


Save this as` run-cluster.sh` and run it from` k6-workflow` :


```text
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set   -euo   pipefail
:   "${  SNAPSHOT_ID  :?  Set   SNAPSHOT_ID  }"
:   "${  CLUSTER  :?  Set   CLUSTER  }"
:   "${  NAMESPACE  :?  Set   NAMESPACE  }"
:   "${  KUBE_CONTEXT  :?  Set   KUBE_CONTEXT  }"
SUT_PORT  =  ${SUT_PORT  :-  8080}
REPORT_ID  =  ""
FORWARD_PID  =  ""
cleanup  () {
status  =  $?
trap   -   EXIT
if   [[   -n   "  $FORWARD_PID  "   ]];   then
kill   "  $FORWARD_PID  "   2>  /dev/null   ||   true
wait   "  $FORWARD_PID  "   2>  /dev/null   ||   true
fi
if   [[   -n   "  $REPORT_ID  "   ]];   then
speedctl   infra   cancel-replay   "  $REPORT_ID  "   ||   true
fi
exit   "  $status  "
}
trap   cleanup   EXIT
trap   'exit 130'   INT
trap   'exit 143'   TERM


REPORT_ID  =  $(  speedctl   infra   replay   \
--snapshot-id   "  $SNAPSHOT_ID  "   \
--cluster   "  $CLUSTER  "   --namespace   "  $NAMESPACE  "   --service   gateway   \
--test-config-id   k6-tutorial-external-driver   --id-only  )


speedctl   wait   replay   "  $REPORT_ID  "   --for   mocks-ready   \
--cluster   "  $CLUSTER  "   --namespace   "  $NAMESPACE  "   \
--timeout   10m   --poll-interval   5s


kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   port-forward   -n   "  $NAMESPACE  "   \
service/gateway   "  $SUT_PORT  :80"   >   port-forward.log   2>&1   &
FORWARD_PID  =  $!
ready  =  false
for   attempt   in   {  1..30}  ;   do
if   !   kill   -0   "  $FORWARD_PID  "   2>  /dev/null  ;   then
cat   port-forward.log
exit   1
fi
if   curl   --noproxy   '*'   --max-time   2   --fail   --silent   \
"http://127.0.0.1:  $SUT_PORT  /payment/"   >   /dev/null  ;   then
ready  =  true
break
fi
sleep   1
done
if   [[   "  $ready  "   !=   true   ]];   then
cat   port-forward.log
exit   1
fi
k6   run   --env   "BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:  $SUT_PORT  "   k6.js
```


```text
bash   run-cluster.sh
```


Starting the port-forward after` mocks-ready` matters: attaching mocks can roll the gateway pod and disconnect an earlier port-forward. The cleanup trap cancels the replay when k6 finishes or fails.


In the Speedscale report, verify that payment requests matched recorded responses and that no backend requests passed through. k6’s successful payment body check verifies the gateway’s response; the mock match data verifies where the backend response came from.


## Mock backends locally with proxymock


Stay in` k6-demo/k6-workflow` . Pull the same snapshot into local files:


```text
proxymock   cloud   pull   snapshot   "  $SNAPSHOT_ID  "   --out   ./mocks
```


Start the mock server in this terminal and leave it running:


```text
proxymock   mock   --in   ./mocks   --out   ./mock-results   \
--map   18081=http://payment:80   --no-passthrough
```


NGINX doesn’t use` HTTP_PROXY` or` http_proxy` . The reverse mapping listens on port 18081 and associates requests with the recorded` payment:80` backend.` --no-passthrough` prevents unmatched calls from reaching a real dependency.


In a second terminal, change to the same` k6-demo/k6-workflow` directory. Save this as` local-gateway.conf` :


```text
server   {
listen   8080  ;
location   /payment/   {
proxy_pass   http://host.docker.internal:18081/;
proxy_set_header   Host payment;
}
}
```


Run the gateway locally, with Docker connecting to the mock port on your host:


```text
docker   run   --rm   --name   k6-local-gateway   \
--add-host   host.docker.internal:host-gateway   \
-p   8080:8080   \
--mount   "type=bind,src=  $PWD  /local-gateway.conf,dst=/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf,readonly"   \
nginx:1.27
```


The gateway keeps the original` /payment/` route and sends` Host: payment` to the mock. There is no local payment service. In a third terminal, change to` k6-demo/k6-workflow` and run:


```text
curl   --noproxy   '*'   --max-time   10   --fail   --silent   --show-error   http://127.0.0.1:8080/payment/
k6   run   --env   BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080   k6.js
```


Expect the same payment JSON and all k6 checks to pass. In the proxymock terminal and` mock-results` , confirm payment calls are marked` HIT` (a successful match), with no` MISS` or` PASSTHROUGH` results. A 502 from NGINX usually means it can’t reach the mock listener; a mock miss means the outgoing request differs from the recording.


## Read the results and clean up


In the validation run, each path completed 150 requests and 300 successful checks with no failed HTTP requests. The local responder recorded backend hits, and the cluster report recorded mock matches with no misses or passthrough. Your latency and request counts will depend on the machine and recording.


Compare k6’s request count, failure rate, and p95 latency across runs. Require passing body checks and confirmed mock matches before treating a run as valid. The local example measures a Docker gateway and host mock server; the cluster example includes the port-forward and cluster responder. Those are useful workflow checks, but port-forward results aren’t a measure of cluster capacity. Run k6 inside the cluster or through your normal test ingress for capacity testing.


Mocking isolates the gateway’s behavior from the real payment backend. Backend performance, end-to-end capacity, and the effect of recorded dependency latency require separate test configurations. The local responder returns immediately by default; use` --mock-timing recorded` if you want to include the captured backend delay.


Stop the local mock server with Ctrl+C and stop the Docker gateway:


```text
docker   stop   k6-local-gateway
```


The cluster script already cancels its replay. Once that cleanup has finished, remove only the namespace created for this tutorial:


```text
kubectl   --context   "  $KUBE_CONTEXT  "   delete   namespace   "  $NAMESPACE  "
```


For your own service, keep the same flow:[capture inbound and outbound traffic](https://speedscale.com/blog/definitive-guide-to-traffic-replay/) , export the inbound requests to k6, and[mock the recorded dependencies](https://speedscale.com/features/service-virtualization/) while k6 drives the application. Adapt response assertions and dynamic values to your API before increasing the load.


Ready to try it on your own service?[Install proxymock and record your first traffic](https://docs.speedscale.com/proxymock/getting-started/quickstart/quickstart-cli/) , then export your service’s snapshot to k6 and adapt its response assertions before running a load test.


## Frequently asked questions


### What does the k6 export preserve from the recording?


It turns eligible recorded inbound HTTP requests into a script with their request data. Speedscale transforms are not exported. Review target URLs, credentials, dynamic values, and request ordering, then add your own load schedule and assertions. In k6, checks need thresholds if a failed check should produce a failing test exit code.


### When should dependencies be mocked or left real?


Mock a dependency to measure the application with controlled responses. Leave an isolated test instance real when its own behavior, state, or capacity is part of the question. Keep captured outbound exchanges for the mocks even though only inbound requests drive k6. Confirm mock hits and investigate misses before trusting the load results.


### Can I run the same workflow locally and in Kubernetes?


Yes, but the setup differs. This tutorial captures and exports a snapshot through Speedscale, then uses either cluster responders or a local proxymock listener for dependency responses. The local replay path does not remove those earlier cluster steps. Port-forwarded cluster results validate the workflow; use an appropriate in-cluster driver or test ingress for capacity measurements.


Sources:[Speedscale k6 export](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/integrations/export/grafana/) ,[k6 thresholds](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/thresholds/) ,[Configure dependency mocks](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/replay/mocks/) ,[proxymock architecture](https://docs.speedscale.com/proxymock/how-it-works/architecture/) ,[Generator sizing and bottlenecks](https://docs.speedscale.com/reference/generator-sizing-guide/) .
